definition: The study of matter and the changes it undergoes.
The cycle of observing, asking a question, forming a hypothesis, experimenting and analyzing that scientists use to learn about nature.
An observation that describes a quality in words, not numbers, such as "the solution turned pink."
An observation that is a measurement: a number with a unit, such as "the volume is 25.0 mL."
A tentative, testable explanation of an observation. A good hypothesis is falsifiable: an experiment could show it is wrong.
A short statement, often an equation, that describes what always happens. A law says what happens; it does not explain why.
A well-tested explanation of why nature behaves the way it does, such as the atomic theory.
Mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction: atoms are only rearranged, so the total mass of the products equals the total mass of the reactants.
A way of writing a number as N × 10<sup>n</sup>, where N is at least 1 but less than 10 and n is a positive or negative integer.

definition: The international system of measurement based on the metric system; its base units include the meter, kilogram, second, kelvin and mole.
source_file: inherited: LibreTexts 1.2.2 The Basic Units of Measurement (not in drafts)

definition: A prefix such as kilo- (1000), centi- (1/100), milli- (1/1000) or micro- (1/1,000,000) that changes the size of a metric unit by a power of ten.
source_file: inherited: LibreTexts 1.2.2 The Basic Units of Measurement (not in drafts)

definition: All the certain digits in a measurement plus one estimated digit. Nonzero and middle zeros count, leading zeros never count, and trailing zeros count only when a decimal point is shown (2500 has 2; 2500. has 4).
source_file: inherited: LibreTexts 1.3.1 Significant Figures (not in drafts)

definition: Zeros after all the nonzero digits. Without a decimal point they are not significant (500 has 1 significant figure); with a decimal point they are (500. has 3; 620.0 has 4).
source_file: inherited: LibreTexts 1.3.1 Significant Figures (not in drafts)

definition: A number that is counted or defined (12 eggs; 1 kg = 1000 g) rather than measured; it has unlimited significant figures and never limits a calculated answer.
source_file: inherited: LibreTexts 1.3.1 Significant Figures (not in drafts)

definition: How close a measured value is to the true value.
source_file: inherited: LibreTexts 1.3.1 Significant Figures (not in drafts)

definition: How close repeated measurements are to one another (how reproducible they are).
source_file: inherited: LibreTexts 1.3.1 Significant Figures (not in drafts)

definition: A ratio, equal to 1, that relates two units (such as 100 cm / 1 m) and is used to change a quantity from one unit to another.
source_file: inherited: LibreTexts 1.4.1 Problem Solving and Unit Conversions (not in drafts)

definition: Solving a problem by multiplying the given quantity by conversion factors arranged so the unwanted units cancel and the desired unit remains.
source_file: inherited: LibreTexts 1.4.1 Problem Solving and Unit Conversions (not in drafts)

definition: Anything that has mass and takes up space. Light, heat and sound are forms of energy, not matter.
The smallest particle of an element that still has the properties of that element.
Two or more atoms bonded together as a unit, such as O<sub>2</sub> or H<sub>2</sub>O.
The smallest repeating ratio of ions in an ionic compound, such as one Na<sup>+</sup> and one Cl<sup>−</sup> in NaCl. Ionic compounds are not made of molecules.
A code that lists the elements in a substance, with subscripts that count the atoms of each, such as H<sub>2</sub>O.
A two-atom molecule. Seven elements exist as diatomic molecules when uncombined: H<sub>2</sub>, N<sub>2</sub>, O<sub>2</sub>, F<sub>2</sub>, Cl<sub>2</sub>, Br<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub>.
Matter with a fixed composition in which every particle is the same; it is either an element or a compound.
A pure substance that contains only one kind of atom and cannot be broken down into simpler substances by a chemical change.
A pure substance made of two or more elements chemically bonded in a fixed ratio; it can be broken down into its elements only by a chemical change.
Two or more substances physically combined, not bonded. Its composition can vary and it can be separated by physical means.
A mixture that is uniform throughout, such as saline or air; also called a solution.
A mixture that is not uniform, with regions you (or a microscope) can tell apart, such as salad dressing or whole blood.
The three common forms of matter: solid, liquid and gas.
A state of matter with a definite shape and a definite volume; its particles are closely packed and touching.
A state of matter with a definite volume but no definite shape; its particles touch but can slide past one another, so it flows.
A state of matter with no definite shape or volume; its particles are far apart and fast, so a gas fills its container and is easy to compress.
A property of matter that causes pushes and pulls between particles. It is positive or negative: like charges repel and opposite charges attract.
A property that can be observed or measured without changing the identity of the substance, such as color, melting point or density.
A property that describes how a substance changes into a different substance, such as flammability; it is observed only by trying the change.
A property that depends on how much of the sample you have, such as mass or volume.
A property that is the same for any amount of the substance, such as color, boiling point or density.
A change in form or appearance in which the particles stay the same, such as cutting, dissolving or any change of state.
A change that turns one or more substances into new substances with different compositions and properties; atoms are rearranged, old bonds break and new bonds form.
A solid that forms when two solutions are mixed.
The mass of a substance divided by its volume (d = m/V), often in g/mL or g/cm<sup>3</sup>. It is an intensive property and can be used as a conversion factor between mass and volume.
The theory that elements are made of atoms, atoms of one element are alike, atoms combine in simple whole-number ratios, and atoms are rearranged (not created or destroyed) in reactions.
A compound always contains the same elements in the same proportions by mass, whatever its source.
A negatively charged subatomic particle (charge 1−, mass about 0 amu) found outside the nucleus; electrons are what atoms gain, lose or share in reactions.
The tiny, dense center of an atom that holds all of its positive charge (protons) and almost all of its mass (protons and neutrons).
A subatomic particle in the nucleus with a 1+ charge and a mass of about 1 amu. The number of protons identifies the element.
A subatomic particle in the nucleus with no charge and a mass of about 1 amu.
A unit for the masses of atoms, defined as one-twelfth of the mass of a carbon-12 atom (1 amu = 1.6605 × 10<sup>−24</sup> g).
The number of protons in an atom's nucleus (symbol Z). It defines the element; in a neutral atom it also equals the number of electrons.
A vertical column of the periodic table, numbered 1 to 18. Elements in a group have similar chemical properties.
A horizontal row of the periodic table, numbered 1 to 7.
The elements in groups 1, 2 and 13–18, whose behavior is predictable from their position.
The elements in groups 3–12, in the middle of the periodic table.
An element to the left of the staircase line that is shiny, conducts heat and electricity, and is malleable and ductile; metals tend to lose electrons and form cations.
An element in the upper right of the periodic table (plus hydrogen) that is dull and brittle as a solid and conducts poorly; nonmetals tend to gain electrons.
An element along the staircase line (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te and usually At) with properties between those of metals and nonmetals.
The group 1 metals (Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs): soft, very reactive metals that react with water. Hydrogen sits in group 1 but is not an alkali metal.
The group 2 metals (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba): reactive metals that form 2+ ions.
The group 17 elements (F, Cl, Br, I): very reactive nonmetals that exist as diatomic molecules.
The group 18 elements (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe): very unreactive gases that exist as single atoms because their valence shells are full.
An atom or group of atoms with an overall electric charge because its numbers of protons and electrons are not equal. Only electrons are gained or lost.
A positive ion, formed when an atom loses electrons. Metals usually form cations.
A negative ion, formed when an atom gains electrons. Nonmetals usually form anions.
The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom's nucleus (symbol A).
Atoms of the same element (same atomic number) with different numbers of neutrons, and so different mass numbers, such as chlorine-35 and chlorine-37.
A symbol that shows the mass number as a superscript and the atomic number as a subscript to the left of the element symbol, as in <sup>37</sup><sub>17</sub>Cl; also written chlorine-37 or Cl-37.
The weighted average of the masses of an element's isotopes, using their natural percent abundances; it is the mass shown on the periodic table.
The percentage of an element's atoms in nature that are a given isotope; dividing by 100 gives the fractional abundance.
Energy that travels as a wave of electric and magnetic fields, including radio waves, visible light, X-rays and gamma rays.
The distance from one wave peak to the next (symbol λ). Visible light has wavelengths of about 400 to 700 nm.
The number of wave peaks that pass a point each second (symbol ν), in hertz (Hz = s<sup>−1</sup>). Wavelength and frequency are inversely related.
The speed at which all electromagnetic radiation travels in a vacuum, c = 3.00 × 10<sup>8</sup> m s<sup>−1</sup>; c = λν.
A tiny packet of light energy. Its energy depends only on its frequency (E = hν), so shorter wavelengths carry more energy per photon.
The full range of electromagnetic radiation, from long-wavelength, low-energy radio waves to short-wavelength, high-energy gamma rays; visible light is a narrow band.
Radiation with enough energy to knock electrons off atoms and molecules, making ions; it includes X-rays, gamma rays and alpha and beta particles.
The pattern of separate bright lines of specific wavelengths given off by a glowing gas; each element has its own line spectrum.
Niels Bohr's model of hydrogen, in which the electron moves only in certain allowed energy levels and gives off or absorbs a photon when it jumps between them.
One of the allowed energies an electron can have in an atom, numbered n = 1, 2, 3 and so on; an electron can be in one level or another but never in between.
The lowest-energy arrangement of an atom's electrons.
An arrangement in which an electron has absorbed energy and moved to a higher energy level; when it drops back, it emits a photon.
A main energy level of an atom, numbered n = 1, 2, 3 ...; higher n means electrons farther from the nucleus and higher in energy.
A group of orbitals within a shell, labeled s, p, d or f. Shell n has n kinds of subshells.
A region of space where an electron is most likely to be found. Each orbital holds at most 2 electrons; an s subshell has 1 orbital, p has 3, d has 5 and f has 7.
Electrons fill the lowest-energy orbitals first; for example, 4s fills before 3d.
An orbital holds at most two electrons, and if it holds two they must have opposite spins (↑↓).
When filling orbitals of equal energy, put one electron in each orbital, all with the same spin, before pairing any of them.
A diagram that shows each orbital as a box or line and each electron as an arrow.
A one-line list of the occupied subshells, each with a superscript for its number of electrons, such as 1s<sup>2</sup> 2s<sup>2</sup> 2p<sup>3</sup> for nitrogen.
An electron configuration that replaces the inner electrons with the symbol of the previous noble gas in brackets, such as [Ne] 3s<sup>2</sup> 3p<sup>3</sup> for phosphorus.
The electrons in an atom that are not valence electrons; in a noble-gas configuration, the electrons represented by the bracket.
Having the same electron configuration; Na<sup>+</sup> is isoelectronic with neon and Cl<sup>−</sup> with argon.

The electrons in an atom's outermost (highest-numbered) shell, which are gained, lost or shared in reactions. For main-group elements, groups 1–2 have 1–2 and groups 13–18 have (group number − 10), except helium with 2.
A set of eight valence electrons (ns<sup>2</sup> np<sup>6</sup>), the full valence shell of the noble gases other than helium.
Main-group atoms tend to gain, lose or share electrons until they have eight valence electrons (two for hydrogen and helium).
An element symbol surrounded by dots that represent its valence electrons.
A measure of an atom's size: half the distance between the nuclei of two identical bonded atoms. It increases down a group and decreases across a period.
The energy needed to remove one electron from a gaseous atom, forming a 1+ ion. It increases across a period and decreases down a group.
How readily an element behaves as a metal by losing electrons; it is greatest toward the lower left of the periodic table.
A small number written low after a symbol that tells how many atoms of that element are in the formula; no subscript means 1. Subscripts are never changed when balancing.
A number in front of a formula that counts whole molecules or formula units (or moles of them).
A compound made of ions, usually a metal cation (or NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup>) and an anion, held together by ionic bonds in a crystal lattice.
A compound made only of nonmetals whose atoms share electrons in covalent bonds; it exists as separate molecules.
A compound that releases H<sup>+</sup> ions when dissolved in water; acid formulas usually start with H. Acids taste sour, turn blue litmus red and react with active metals and carbonates.
Dissolved in water, shown by the phase label (aq). A solution with water as the solvent is an aqueous solution.
A compound that contains just two elements, such as NaCl or CO<sub>2</sub>.
A group of atoms bonded together that carries an overall charge and acts as a single unit, such as sulfate, SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup>.
A polyatomic anion that contains oxygen. Names follow a pattern from the -ate ion: per-...-ate (one more O), -ite (one fewer O), hypo-...-ite (two fewer O).
A metal that forms only one ion, so the metal name alone is enough in a compound name (for example, sodium, calcium and aluminum).
A metal, usually a transition metal, that can form more than one ion; its charge is shown with a Roman numeral in the name, as in iron(III) oxide.
An ionic compound whose crystals hold a fixed number of water molecules, written after a raised dot, such as CuSO<sub>4</sub>·5H<sub>2</sub>O (copper(II) sulfate pentahydrate).
Without water; the compound left after the water is driven off a hydrate.
An acid made of hydrogen and one other nonmetal dissolved in water, named hydro- + root + -ic acid, such as hydrochloric acid, HCl(aq).
An acid that contains hydrogen, oxygen and another element; an -ate anion gives an -ic acid and an -ite anion gives an -ous acid, with no hydro- prefix.
The counting unit for particles: 1 mol = 6.0221 × 10<sup>23</sup> particles (atoms, molecules, formula units or ions).
The number of particles in one mole, 6.0221 × 10<sup>23</sup>; it converts between moles and particles.
The sum of the average atomic masses (in amu) of all the atoms in a formula; called molecular mass for a molecule.
The mass of one mole of a substance, in g/mol (g mol<sup>−1</sup>). For an element it is the atomic mass on the periodic table; for a compound it is the formula mass in g/mol.
Using the mole ratios in a balanced equation to answer "how much?": how much product forms, how much reactant is needed, which reactant runs out and how much heat is released.
The attraction between oppositely charged ions formed when electrons transfer from a metal to a nonmetal.
An ionic compound made of a cation (other than H<sup>+</sup>) and an anion (other than OH<sup>−</sup> or O<sup>2−</sup>), such as NaCl; salts form when acids neutralize bases.

A substance that releases OH<sup>−</sup> ions in water (in this course, mostly metal hydroxides) or accepts H<sup>+</sup>. Bases taste bitter, feel slippery, turn red litmus blue and turn phenolphthalein pink.
A huge, repeating three-dimensional array of particles; in an ionic solid each ion is surrounded by ions of opposite charge.
A pair of electrons shared between two atoms, usually two nonmetals.
A drawing of a molecule or polyatomic ion that shows all valence electrons: each shared pair as a line and unshared electrons as pairs of dots.
A pair of valence electrons that belongs to one atom only and is not shared in a bond.
A covalent bond made of two shared pairs of electrons, as in O=O; it is shorter and stronger than a single bond.
A covalent bond made of three shared pairs of electrons, as in N≡N; it is shorter and stronger than a double bond.

synonyms: valence shell electron pair repulsion theory
definition: The theory that the electron groups around a central atom repel each other and spread out as far apart as possible, which predicts the molecule's shape.
Any region of electrons around a central atom: a single, double or triple bond (each counts as one group) or a lone pair.
The arrangement of all electron groups around a central atom: 2 groups linear, 3 trigonal planar, 4 tetrahedral.
The arrangement of the atoms only (not lone pairs) around a central atom, such as linear, bent, trigonal planar, trigonal pyramidal or tetrahedral.
The shape with two electron groups and no lone pairs on the central atom, with a 180° bond angle, as in CO<sub>2</sub>.
The flat shape with three electron groups and no lone pairs on the central atom, with 120° bond angles, as in CH<sub>2</sub>O.
The shape with four electron groups and no lone pairs on the central atom, with 109.5° bond angles, as in CH<sub>4</sub>.
The shape with four electron groups, one of them a lone pair, on the central atom (bond angles slightly less than 109.5°), as in NH<sub>3</sub>.
The shape of a molecule with two bonded atoms and one or two lone pairs on the central atom, as in H<sub>2</sub>O (two lone pairs) and SO<sub>2</sub> (one lone pair).
An atom's ability to attract the shared electrons in a bond toward itself (Pauling scale, about 0.7 to 4.0). It increases across a period and decreases down a group.
A bond in which electrons are shared (almost) equally: an electronegativity difference of 0 to 0.4, as in H–H or C–H.

A bond in which electrons are shared unequally: an electronegativity difference of more than 0.4 up to 2.0, giving the more electronegative atom a partial negative charge (δ−) and the other a partial positive charge (δ+); shown with a dipole arrow pointing toward the more electronegative atom.
A molecule whose bond dipoles do not cancel, leaving a net dipole; usually asymmetrical, with lone pairs on the central atom or different outer atoms (H<sub>2</sub>O, NH<sub>3</sub>).
A molecule with no net dipole, either because it has no polar bonds or because it is symmetrical so its bond dipoles cancel (CO<sub>2</sub>, CCl<sub>4</sub>).
The percent by mass of each element in a compound.
A formula that gives the smallest whole-number ratio of atoms in a compound; glucose, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>12</sub>O<sub>6</sub>, has the empirical formula CH<sub>2</sub>O.
A formula that gives the actual number of each kind of atom in one molecule; it is a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula.

Two or more valid Lewis structures that differ only in where the electrons, not the atoms, are placed; they are drawn with a double-headed arrow between them. The real molecule is one resonance hybrid, a blend of the structures.
A molecule or fragment with an unpaired electron, such as NO or the hydroxyl radical (·OH); radicals are usually very reactive.
A description of a reaction with the reactants on the left, an arrow meaning "react to form," and the products on the right.
A starting substance in a chemical reaction, written on the left of the arrow.
A substance formed in a chemical reaction, written on the right of the arrow.
A chemical equation with the same number of atoms of each element on both sides, as the law of conservation of mass requires; it is balanced by changing coefficients, never subscripts.
A reaction in which two or more reactants form one product: A + B → AB.
A reaction in which one reactant breaks into two or more simpler substances, AB → A + B, usually with heat, light or electricity.
A reaction in which an element replaces one partner in a compound: A + BC → AC + B, such as a metal replacing a metal ion or hydrogen.
A reaction in which two ionic compounds swap partners, AB + CD → AD + CB; it happens only if a precipitate, water (or another weak electrolyte) or a gas forms.

A rapid reaction of a carbon-based fuel with oxygen that releases heat and light. Complete combustion (enough O<sub>2</sub>) gives CO<sub>2</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>O; incomplete combustion (too little O<sub>2</sub>) also forms carbon monoxide and soot.
A substance that forms ions in water, so its solution conducts electricity.
A substance that breaks apart completely into ions in water: soluble ionic compounds, strong acids and strong bases.
A substance that forms only a few ions in water, so most of it stays as molecules, such as acetic acid and ammonia.
A substance that dissolves as whole molecules and forms no ions, such as sugar, ethanol or urea.
Not dissolving appreciably in water; an insoluble ionic compound stays a solid because its ions attract each other more strongly than they attract water.
Rules (on the course green sheet) that predict whether an ionic compound dissolves in water; any compound with a group 1 ion or ammonium is soluble.
A double-displacement reaction in which one product is an insoluble solid (a precipitate).
An equation that writes every substance as a neutral formula.
An equation that splits every aqueous strong electrolyte into its ions; solids, liquids, gases and weak electrolytes stay together.
An ion that appears unchanged on both sides of a complete ionic equation and is cancelled out.
An equation that shows only the species that actually change, after the spectator ions are cancelled.
A reaction of an acid with a base in which H<sup>+</sup> and OH<sup>−</sup> combine to form water and the remaining ions form a salt: acid + base → water + salt.
A double-displacement reaction that releases a gas, often because a product such as H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> breaks down into CO<sub>2</sub> and water.
A reaction in which electrons move from one substance to another; oxidation and reduction always happen together.
The loss of electrons; the oxidation number increases ("LEO": lose electrons, oxidation; "OIL": oxidation is loss).
The gain of electrons; the oxidation number decreases ("GER": gain electrons, reduction; "RIG": reduction is gain).
A bookkeeping charge assigned to each atom, by rules applied in order, to track electrons in a reaction; an atom in a pure element has oxidation number 0.
The reactant that is reduced; it causes the other substance to be oxidized.
The reactant that is oxidized; it causes the other substance to be reduced.
One part of a redox reaction, showing only the electrons lost (oxidation) or only the electrons gained (reduction).
A list of metals in order of how easily they give up electrons. A free metal displaces the ions of any metal below it, and metals above hydrogen react with acids to release H<sub>2</sub>.
A device in which the oxidation and reduction half-reactions happen in separate places, so electrons travel through an outside wire and can power a device.
The electrode where oxidation happens.
The electrode where reduction happens.
A ratio from the coefficients of a balanced equation (such as 1 mol N<sub>2</sub> : 3 mol H<sub>2</sub>) that converts moles of one substance to moles of another; it is exact.
The moles of solute per liter of solution (M = mol/L); a conversion factor between liters of solution and moles of solute.
0 °C (273 K) and 1 atm.
The volume of one mole of a gas; at STP it is 22.4 L for any ideal gas.
The reactant that runs out first and so limits the amount of product that can form; it is the one that makes the least product.
A reactant that is left over when the limiting reactant is used up.
The maximum amount of product predicted by stoichiometry from the limiting reactant.
The amount of product actually collected and weighed.
The actual yield divided by the theoretical yield, times 100%.
The heat absorbed or released by a reaction at constant pressure (ΔH), usually in kJ; it goes with the moles in the balanced equation as written.
Releasing heat to the surroundings, which warm up; ΔH (and q for the system) is negative.
Absorbing heat from the surroundings, which cool down; ΔH (and q for the system) is positive.
A balanced chemical equation written with its ΔH.
The Calorie on a food label (capital C), equal to one kilocalorie: 1 Cal = 1 kcal = 1000 cal = 4.184 kJ.
The capacity to do work or to supply heat.
Energy that flows from a hotter object to a colder one because of their difference in temperature.
The energy of motion; the faster something moves, the more kinetic energy it has.
Stored energy due to position or composition; chemical potential energy is stored in the arrangement of atoms in bonds and in the attractions between particles.
A measure of how hot or cold something is; on the particle level, a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles.
Energy cannot be created or destroyed; it can only change from one form to another or move from one object to another.
The SI temperature scale, which starts at absolute zero; a kelvin is the same size as a Celsius degree, and K = °C + 273.15. It is written K, never °K, and is never negative.
The lowest possible temperature, 0 K = −273.15 °C, where particles have the least possible energy.
The SI unit of energy (1 J = 1 kg·m<sup>2</sup>/s<sup>2</sup>); 1 kJ = 1000 J.
A unit of energy first defined as the heat needed to raise 1 g of water by 1 °C; today defined exactly as 1 cal = 4.184 J.
The part of the world being studied, such as a reaction or a melting ice cube.
Everything outside the system, such as the water, the container and the air.
The heat needed to raise the temperature of 1 g of a substance by 1 °C, in J/(g·°C); for liquid water it is 4.184 J/(g·°C). Used in q = mcΔT.
An insulated container in which heat moves between objects but does not escape, so heat lost by the hot object equals heat gained by the cold one.
The conversion of a substance from one state to another without changing its identity; the temperature stays constant during the change.
The change from solid to liquid; it absorbs heat (endothermic).
The change from liquid to solid; it releases heat (exothermic).
The change from liquid to gas, by evaporation at the surface or by boiling throughout the liquid; it absorbs heat (endothermic).
The change from gas to liquid; it releases heat (exothermic).
The change directly from solid to gas without melting, as dry ice does; it absorbs heat. The reverse, gas directly to solid, is deposition.
The heat needed to melt a substance at its melting point; for water, 6.02 kJ/mol (334 J/g).
The heat needed to vaporize a liquid at its boiling point; for water, 40.7 kJ/mol (2260 J/g).
A graph of a substance's temperature against heat added: sloped segments where one state warms (q = mcΔT) and flat plateaus where a phase change happens (q = nΔH).
Attractions between separate molecules (or between ions and molecules). They are not bonds; they control melting points, boiling points and solubility.
Attractions between all atoms and molecules, caused by brief instantaneous dipoles that induce dipoles in neighbors; stronger for particles with more electrons (larger molar mass).
Attractions between the δ+ end of one polar molecule and the δ− end of another.
An especially strong dipole–dipole attraction between an H atom bonded directly to N, O or F and a lone pair on another N, O or F.
The attraction between an ion and a polar molecule, as when water molecules surround Na<sup>+</sup> and Cl<sup>−</sup> ions in solution.
The energy needed to increase the surface area of a liquid; it is high when intermolecular forces are strong, as in water.
A liquid's resistance to flow; stronger intermolecular forces and long, tangling molecules make a liquid more viscous.
A liquid rising in a narrow tube, which happens when the liquid's attraction to the tube walls (adhesion) is stronger than its attraction to itself (cohesion).
A solid whose particles are arranged in a regular, repeating three-dimensional pattern (a crystal lattice), such as salt, ice and metals.
A solid whose particles are jumbled, with no long-range order, such as glass and many plastics.
A crystalline solid of cations and anions held by ionic bonds: high melting point, hard but brittle, conducts only when melted or dissolved.
A crystalline solid of molecules held by intermolecular forces: low melting point, soft, does not conduct.
A crystalline solid of atoms joined by covalent bonds throughout, such as diamond and quartz: very high melting point and very hard.
A crystalline solid of metal cations in a "sea" of electrons: shiny, malleable and a good conductor of heat and electricity.
The escape of molecules from the surface of a liquid into the gas phase, which can happen at any temperature and cools the liquid left behind.
The pressure of a vapor in dynamic equilibrium with its liquid in a closed container. It increases with temperature and is lower when intermolecular forces are stronger.
A state in which two opposite processes run at the same rate, so nothing appears to change even though both continue.
The temperature at which a liquid's vapor pressure equals the pressure above it, so bubbles of vapor form throughout the liquid. It changes with outside pressure.

The model of an ideal gas: tiny particles in constant, random motion with mostly empty space between them, elastic collisions, no attractions, and an average kinetic energy proportional to the Kelvin temperature.
A gas that behaves exactly as kinetic molecular theory describes.
Force per unit area; for a gas, the result of particles hitting the container walls.
The pressure exerted by the weight of the air above us, about 1 atm at sea level; it decreases with altitude.
At constant temperature and amount of gas, pressure and volume are inversely related: P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>.
At constant pressure and amount of gas, volume and Kelvin temperature are directly related: V<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>1</sub> = V<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>2</sub>.
At constant volume and amount of gas, pressure and Kelvin temperature are directly related: P<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>2</sub>.
At constant pressure and temperature, volume and moles of gas are directly related; equal volumes of gases at the same T and P contain equal numbers of particles.
P<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub>/T<sub>1</sub> = P<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>/T<sub>2</sub>, used when pressure, volume and temperature all change for a fixed amount of gas.
A relationship in which two variables move in the same direction (one doubles, the other doubles); written as a ratio, A<sub>1</sub>/B<sub>1</sub> = A<sub>2</sub>/B<sub>2</sub>.
A relationship in which two variables move in opposite directions (one doubles, the other halves); written as a product, A<sub>1</sub>B<sub>1</sub> = A<sub>2</sub>B<sub>2</sub>.
PV = nRT, which relates the pressure, volume, moles and Kelvin temperature of a gas.
The constant R in PV = nRT; with P in atm, V in liters and T in kelvins, R = 0.082058 L·atm/(mol·K).
The pressure one gas in a mixture would exert if it were alone in the same container at the same temperature.
The total pressure of a gas mixture is the sum of the partial pressures of its gases: P<sub>total</sub> = P<sub>1</sub> + P<sub>2</sub> + ...
The moles of one component divided by the total moles in a mixture; a gas's partial pressure equals its mole fraction times the total pressure.
A homogeneous mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent.
The component of a solution present in the larger amount; the substance that does the dissolving.
The substance dissolved in a solvent.
The rule that polar and ionic solutes dissolve in polar solvents and nonpolar solutes dissolve in nonpolar solvents.
Describes two liquids that mix in all proportions, such as ethanol and water.
Describes two liquids that do not mix and separate into layers, such as oil and water.
The maximum amount of a substance that dissolves in a given amount of solvent at a given temperature, often in grams per 100 g of water.
A solution that holds less solute than the maximum; more solute will dissolve.
A solution that holds the maximum amount of solute; added solute stays undissolved.
An unstable solution that holds more than the maximum amount of solute; stirring or a seed crystal makes the extra solute crystallize.
At constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid.
A concentration equal to the mass of solute divided by the mass of solution, times 100%.
A concentration equal to grams of solute per 100 mL of solution; 0.9% NaCl contains 0.9 g NaCl in every 100 mL.
A concentration equal to the volume of solute divided by the volume of solution, times 100%, used for liquids mixed with liquids.
A concentration for very dilute solutions that works like a percent but per million parts of solution instead of per hundred.
Adding solvent to lower a solution's concentration; the moles of solute do not change, so M<sub>1</sub>V<sub>1</sub> = M<sub>2</sub>V<sub>2</sub>.
A method that finds the unknown concentration of a solution by reacting a measured volume of it with a solution of known concentration.
The solution of known concentration that is added from the buret in a titration.
A dye whose color depends on how acidic or basic a solution is, such as phenolphthalein, litmus or red cabbage indicator.
The point in a titration where the indicator changes color (for phenolphthalein, the first faint pink that lasts), showing that the moles of base match the moles of acid.
Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent.
A property that depends on the number of dissolved particles, not their identity, such as freezing point depression, boiling point elevation and osmotic pressure.
The number of particles each formula unit of solute forms in solution (i = 1 for glucose, 2 for NaCl, 3 for CaCl<sub>2</sub>).
The lowering of a solvent's freezing point by dissolved particles.
The raising of a solvent's boiling point by dissolved particles.
The net flow of water across a semipermeable membrane from the side with lower solute (particle) concentration to the side with higher solute concentration.
The pressure needed to stop the flow of water across a semipermeable membrane by osmosis.
Having the same particle concentration as a cell, so there is no net water flow; 0.9% NaCl (normal saline) is isotonic.
Having a lower particle concentration than a cell; water flows into the cell, and red blood cells can swell and burst (hemolysis).
Having a higher particle concentration than a cell; water flows out, and the cell shrinks (crenation).
A dye on paper strips that turns red in acid and blue in base ("BRA": blue turns red in acid); it shows only acid or base, not strength.
An indicator that is colorless in acidic and neutral solutions and pink in basic solutions (above about pH 8).
A substance that produces hydrogen ions, H<sup>+</sup>, when it dissolves in water.
A substance that produces hydroxide ions, OH<sup>−</sup>, when it dissolves in water.
H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, the form H<sup>+</sup> (a bare proton) takes in water by bonding to a water molecule.
A proton (H<sup>+</sup>) donor.
A proton (H<sup>+</sup>) acceptor.
The species left after an acid donates a proton; it has one fewer H and one more negative charge.
The species formed when a base accepts a proton; it has one more H and one more positive charge.
Two species that differ by exactly one H<sup>+</sup>, such as NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> and NH<sub>3</sub>; every Brønsted–Lowry reaction has two pairs.
Able to act as either an acid or a base, depending on what it reacts with, as water is.
An acid that ionizes completely in water. The six to memorize are HCl, HBr, HI, HNO<sub>3</sub>, HClO<sub>4</sub> and H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>.
An acid that ionizes only slightly in water, so most of it stays as molecules; any acid not on the strong list, such as HF, acetic acid and carbonic acid.
A soluble metal hydroxide that dissociates completely into metal ions and OH<sup>−</sup>: the group 1 hydroxides and the hydroxides of Ca, Sr and Ba.
A base that accepts protons from water only to a small extent, such as ammonia, amines and bicarbonate.

The reaction of water with itself, H<sub>2</sub>O + H<sub>2</sub>O ⇄ H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup> + OH<sup>−</sup>; in pure water at 25 °C, [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] = [OH<sup>−</sup>] = 1.0 × 10<sup>−7</sup> M.
K<sub>w</sub> = [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>][OH<sup>−</sup>] = 1.0 × 10<sup>−14</sup> at 25 °C in any water solution, so the two concentrations are inversely related.
A solution in which [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] is greater than [OH<sup>−</sup>] (greater than 1.0 × 10<sup>−7</sup> M at 25 °C); pH below 7.
A solution in which [OH<sup>−</sup>] is greater than [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] ([H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] less than 1.0 × 10<sup>−7</sup> M at 25 °C); pH above 7.
A solution in which [H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>] = [OH<sup>−</sup>] = 1.0 × 10<sup>−7</sup> M at 25 °C; pH 7.00.
The negative base-10 logarithm of the hydronium ion concentration, pH = −log[H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>]. Lower pH means more acidic, and each pH unit is a tenfold change.
The negative logarithm of the hydroxide ion concentration, pOH = −log[OH<sup>−</sup>]; at 25 °C, pH + pOH = 14.00.
A blood pH below 7.35 (blood too acidic); respiratory acidosis comes from breathing too little, which lets CO<sub>2</sub> build up.
A blood pH above 7.45 (blood too basic); respiratory alkalosis comes from breathing too fast, which blows off CO<sub>2</sub>.
A solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added; it contains a weak acid and its conjugate base (or a weak base and its conjugate acid).
The amount of acid or base a buffer can absorb before its pH changes sharply.
How fast a reactant is used up or a product forms, usually measured as a change in concentration per unit of time.
The idea that a reaction happens only when reactant particles collide with enough energy and the right orientation.
The minimum energy colliding particles need to break bonds and start a reaction; the height of the energy hill above the reactants.
A substance that speeds up a reaction without being used up, by providing a path with a lower activation energy. It does not shift an equilibrium.
A biological catalyst, usually a protein, shaped to bind one particular reactant (its substrate).
A reaction that runs in both directions, the forward reaction (reactants → products, left to right) and the reverse reaction (products → reactants, right to left), written with a double arrow ⇄.
The state in which the forward and reverse reactions run at the same rate, so the concentrations no longer change. The concentrations are constant but usually not equal.
The value of the equilibrium constant expression at equilibrium; written without units. A large K favors products and a small K favors reactants.
The ratio of product concentrations over reactant concentrations, each raised to the power of its coefficient in the balanced equation; pure solids and pure liquids are left out.
When a system at equilibrium is disturbed by a stress (a change in concentration, temperature, or pressure or volume), it shifts in the direction that partly relieves the stress.
The equilibrium constant for a weak acid giving up H<sup>+</sup> to water; the larger K<sub>a</sub>, the stronger the weak acid.
The equilibrium constant for a weak base accepting H<sup>+</sup> from water.
The equilibrium constant for a slightly soluble ionic solid dissolving: the product of the ion concentrations, each raised to its coefficient.
The decrease in a salt's solubility when an ion it already contains is added, because the equilibrium shifts left (Le Chatelier's principle).
The spontaneous emission of radiation by an unstable nucleus.
An isotope whose nucleus is radioactive; carbon-12 and carbon-13 are stable, but carbon-14 is a radioisotope.
An older unit of activity (how many nuclei in a sample decay each second): 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10<sup>10</sup> decays per second.
The SI unit of activity: 1 Bq = 1 decay per second.
The SI unit of absorbed dose (radiation energy absorbed per kilogram of tissue): 1 Gy = 1 J/kg = 100 rad.
The SI unit of equivalent dose (absorbed dose adjusted for how much harm that kind of radiation does to the body): 1 Sv = 100 rem; doses are usually given in millisieverts (mSv).
An equation for a nuclear change in which both the mass numbers (top) and the atomic numbers (bottom) add up to the same totals on each side.
A helium nucleus (2 protons and 2 neutrons) given off in alpha decay; mass number 4, charge 2+. It is stopped by paper or the outer layer of skin.
Radioactive decay in which a nucleus gives off an alpha particle, so its mass number drops by 4 and its atomic number by 2.
A high-energy electron made in the nucleus and given off in beta decay, written <sup>0</sup><sub>−1</sub>e.
Radioactive decay in which a neutron changes into a proton and an electron, and the electron is thrown out as a beta particle; the atomic number rises by 1.
The antimatter partner of the electron, with the same mass and a positive charge, written <sup>0</sup><sub>+1</sub>e.
Radioactive decay in which a proton changes into a neutron and a positron, which leaves the nucleus; the atomic number drops by 1.
A nuclear change in which the nucleus pulls in one of its atom's inner electrons, which combines with a proton to make a neutron.
High-energy electromagnetic radiation given off by a nucleus that has extra energy; it changes neither the mass number nor the atomic number.
Describes a nucleus waiting to release extra energy as a gamma ray, shown by an m after the mass number, as in technetium-99m.
How far radiation travels into matter before it is stopped; gamma rays penetrate most and alpha particles least.
The time it takes for half of the radioactive nuclei in a sample to decay; after each half-life, half of what was left remains.
Finding the age of once-living material from how much of its carbon-14 (half-life 5730 years) has decayed since the organism died.
The splitting of a heavy nucleus into two smaller nuclei, which converts a little mass into a great deal of energy.
A self-sustaining series of fissions in which neutrons released by one fission cause more fissions.
The smallest amount of fissionable material that can keep a chain reaction going.
A device in which a fission chain reaction is kept steady, with on average one neutron from each fission causing another fission.
The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus, which releases even more energy per gram of fuel than fission.
The radiation everyone is exposed to all the time, from cosmic rays, radioactive elements in rocks and soil, potassium-40 in the body, and radon.
From a small source, the radiation dose rate falls with the square of the distance: doubling the distance cuts it to one-fourth.
A radioisotope, often attached to a molecule the body handles in a known way, given in a tiny amount so its location can be imaged.
An imaging method that detects the gamma rays made when positrons from a tracer, usually fluorine-18 fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG), meet electrons in the body.
